wifiPanel.title: Hand the network "{ssid}" to the hornets
wifiPanel.intro: The network and password come from the fields above (save them first). Choose how to hand them over, and to which hornets.

stage.title: Prepare a spare network
stage.what: Nothing is switched or restarted: the hornet stays on its current network and only remembers this one as a spare. It moves to it by itself when it can no longer join its current one, that is, after you change the name or password on the router.
stage.steps: Choose the hornets below and press "Prepare a spare network"|Wait in Events for "spare network saved" from each|Change the network name or password on the router|In a minute or two the hornets move by themselves, Events show "now on ..."
stage.when: Works for changing the password of the same network too. Safe: while you have not touched the router, nothing changes.

switch.title: Switch now (a trial)
switch.what: The hornet restarts at once and tries this network. If it reaches the hive, the network becomes its main one and the old one stays as the spare. If not within a minute, it goes back to the old one by itself.
switch.steps: The new network must already work next to the old one (for example a second name on the router)|Choose ONE hornet and press "Switch"|Wait in Events: "now on ..." or "network did not work, the old one stayed"|If all is well, switch the others
switch.when: Not for changing the password of the same network: while the router knows only one password, the board cannot test the new one.

wifiPanel.choose: Which hornets (only those online and awake)
wifiPanel.asleep: asleep, the command would not reach it
wifiPanel.oldFirmware: old firmware: prepare it over USB or update it
wifiPanel.summaryStage: What will happen: {names} will remember the network "{ssid}" as a spare. Nothing is switched or restarted.
wifiPanel.summarySwitch: What will happen: {names} will restart now and try the network "{ssid}". If they do not reach the hive within a minute they go back to the old one.
wifiPanel.switchWarning: If you have already changed the network or password on the router, the old network does not work and the board has nowhere to go back to: it will have to be fixed over USB.
wifiPanel.confirmStage: Remember the network "{ssid}" as a spare on: {names}? Nothing is switched.
wifiPanel.confirmSwitch: Restart {names} and try the network "{ssid}"? If they do not reach the hive within a minute, they go back to the old one.
wifiPanel.afterStage: Next: wait for "spare network saved" from every hornet, then change the router.
wifiPanel.afterSwitch: Next: in a minute look at "Wi-Fi switch" of each hornet: "now on" or "the old one stayed".

swarm.removeConfirm: Remove “{name}”? The board loses access to the hive; its history stays.
swarm.replaceHint: New board for {id}: flash it and enter this code in the wizard's setup step (or with the enroll command). The old board loses access.
swarm.sleepSaved: Saved. The hornet applies it at its next wake-up
swarm.sleepHint: For battery hornets: wakes, sends a reading and sleeps. Needs a GPIO16–RST jumper (docs/hornet-esp01-battery.md)
swarm.pinsSaved: Saved. The hornet applies it as soon as it gets the new config: right away if online, or at its next wake-up
swarm.pinsRejected: Pins not saved: a conflict or a bad number
swarm.pinsNone: No pins to set for this type
swarm.updateConfirm: Update “{name}” over the air: {from} → {to}? The hornet downloads the firmware, restarts and reports the result.
swarm.updateRisk: The ESP-01 keeps the new image beside the old one and cannot roll back: if power fails during the copy, the board must be reflashed over USB. Update one hornet first.
swarm.updateStarted: Update started: progress shows in events
swarm.updateRefused: The update was not started (check the board, the version and the hive address in Settings)
swarm.pinsNotNumber: {field}: '{value}' is not a number. Enter the GPIO number in digits (A0 on the ESP8266 is 17)
swarm.ratioInvalid: Divider ratio: a number above 0 and up to 100, e.g. 5.7

pinHelp.onewire: 1-Wire bus for DS18B20 sensors (meteo and heat roles). GPIO number.
pinHelp.onewireEsp8266: NodeMCU and D1 mini default: D5 = GPIO14.
pinHelp.sda: I2C data line for the BME280 and the display (meteo and heat roles). GPIO number.
pinHelp.sdaEsp8266: NodeMCU and D1 mini default: D2 = GPIO4.
pinHelp.scl: I2C clock line for the BME280 and the display (meteo and heat roles). GPIO number.
pinHelp.sclEsp8266: NodeMCU and D1 mini default: D1 = GPIO5.
pinHelp.relay: Output to the relay module. GPIO number.
pinHelp.relayEsp8266: NodeMCU and D1 mini default: D6 = GPIO12. Numbering: D1=5, D2=4, D5=14, D6=12, D7=13.
pinHelp.relayEsp32cam: ESP32-CAM default: GPIO4, the white flash LED; a floodlight relay can share it. GPIO12 (the board will not boot if it is high at power-up) and GPIO33 (red LED) are free too.
pinHelp.button: Local button that toggles the relay, shorts the pin to ground. GPIO number.
pinHelp.buttonEsp8266: NodeMCU default: D3 = GPIO0, the FLASH button on the board.
pinHelp.vbat: Battery or supply voltage through a divider. Works in the meteo, relay and heat roles and arrives as the Battery voltage metric (V), usable in rules. Empty turns it off. Set the divider ratio too.
pinHelp.vbatEsp8266: The ESP8266 has one analog input, A0: enter 17.
pinHelp.vbatEsp32c3: On the ESP32-C3 the ADC is on GPIO0–GPIO4.
pinHelp.ratio:
Voltage divider ratio: (R1 + R2) / R2, R1 being the upper leg (to +), R2 the lower one (to ground). Voltage = pin reading × ratio. Empty = 1.
Example: up to 15 V with R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, ratio 5.7.
+12V → R1 47k → A0 → R2 10k → ground.
Keep the pin at or below 3.2 V (NodeMCU, D1 mini) or 3.3 V (ESP32).
Fine tuning: new ratio = current × (multimeter / hive reading).
pinHelp.dht: Data pin of a DHT11/DHT22 (roles meteo and heat, when the thermometer is a DHT). GPIO number.
pinHelp.dhtEsp8266: Usually GPIO2 on the ESP-01. On NodeMCU and D1 mini, D5 = GPIO14 or D7 = GPIO13 will do.
pinHelp.thermometer: What the thermometer is: DS18B20s (one or more on the 1-Wire bus) or one DHT11/DHT22, which also gives humidity. DHT11 and DHT22 are read differently: pick the wrong one and the log says "DHT read failed". "The board's" is a DHT11 on the ESP-01S DHT11 module and a DS18B20 elsewhere.

swarm.updateAvailable: New firmware available: update over the air
swarm.replaceTitle: Replace the board: move this hornet to another board (the old one is cut off)
swarm.fwNone: The hive has no {env} firmware. Build it (pio run in firmware) and deploy the hive: firmware reaches the hive with it.
swarm.fwBecome: another type: becomes "{type}" with the same pins and history; choose what it is used for after the restart
swarm.becomeConfirm: Flash "{name}" over the air to the "{type}" type? The hornet downloads it, restarts and is a "{type}" from then on, with the same pins and history. Choose what it is used for (thermometer, relay, heater) under Pins after the restart.
swarm.fwNoNewer: Nothing newer on the hive. To get a fresh one: build the firmware (pio run in firmware) and deploy the hive.
swarm.fwOffline: The hornet is offline: it can be updated once it is back.
swarm.replaceConfirm: Replace the board of '{id}'? The wizard opens: type and name are known and the code is issued. Flash the new board and enter the code. The hornet moves to the new board with the same name, history and settings; the old board loses access. Updating firmware is another button, the chip one.
swarm.updateUnsigned: The image is not signed (built without the signing key): a hornet that only takes signed firmware will refuse it. See docs/ota.md.

rollout.title: Update all outdated over the air
rollout.intro: Hornets are updated one at a time: the next starts only after the previous one came back with the new version. On the first failure the hive stops and reports to Events and Telegram, so a bad build does not reach every board. You may close the page: the update runs on the hive.
rollout.asleep: asleep: switch it to "awake" for the update
rollout.confirmNoRollback: Update the ESP8266 boards too (D1 mini, NodeMCU, ESP-01). They cannot roll back: if the new firmware does not start or power is lost while it is copied, the board has to be flashed over USB. They go last, after all the others.
rollout.summary: To update: {n}. Up to a few minutes each.
rollout.confirm: Update over the air, one at a time: {names}?
rollout.nothing: The ticked hornets already run the new firmware
rollout.stopConfirm: Stop the update? The hornet updating now finishes on its own, the hive leaves the rest alone.

state.stopping: stopping: waiting for the current hornet

why.timeout: did not come back with the new version in 10 minutes

rollout.failedHint: Check the hornet and its update event in Events. Update the rest again once it is sorted out.

swarm.deceasedHint: Removed hornets are hidden, but their records and history are kept. Turn it on to bring one back to life on a new board.
swarm.reviveTitle: Bring this hornet back to life on a new board: same name and history
swarm.reviveConfirm: Revive '{id}' on a new board? The wizard opens: the code is issued, just flash the board and enter the code. Name, history and settings are kept.
swarm.replaceTasmotaConfirm: Replace the board of '{id}'? A new login and console lines are issued. The previous login stops working.
swarm.relayUnknownTitle: {channel}: state unknown, press to turn on
swarm.sortHint: Place in the list: lower comes first, 0…9999
swarm.sortInvalid: The place is a whole number from 0 to 9999
swarm.fwUsbHint: Connect the board to this computer with a USB cable, press Flash and choose the port. The board's settings (Wi-Fi, hive address, name) are kept: do not tick 'Erase device' in the flashing window. The hornet stays the same, no board replacement needed. When the board is offline this is the only way.
swarm.pinsUnsetHint: the board has none, set it by hand
swarm.waitConfirm: "{name}" is asleep on battery and does not hear commands now. The hive remembers the update to {to} and sends it when the hornet next wakes. It will not go back to sleep until the firmware is installed, so it stays up once for a long while and spends some charge. Continue?
swarm.waitQueued: The update waits for the hornet to wake up
swarm.sleepHelp:
Sleep: how long the hornet sleeps between readings. It wakes, sends a reading and sleeps again, and applies a change at its next wake-up.

Never sleeps: for mains power. Always connected, commands arrive at once.

Deep: the board almost switches off, a battery lasts long. Needs a GPIO16–RST jumper (docs/hornet-esp01-battery.md). Commands do not reach it while it sleeps; a firmware update waits for the wake-up.

Light: stays on Wi‑Fi, commands arrive at once, no jumper, but it saves less.

features.title: Used for
features.hint: What is wired to this hornet. Pins, readings and buttons below follow the choice.

help.thermometer: A temperature sensor: DS18B20s on the 1-Wire bus or a DHT11/DHT22. Which one, and on which pin, is set with the pins below
help.bme280: Temperature, humidity and pressure over I2C (sda and scl pins). On the ESP-01 it shares GPIO0 with the relay
help.relay: A relay switched by buttons, rules and Telegram (relay pin)
help.heater: The relay heats: the hornet keeps the temperature within the limits below by itself, even without the hive. Needs a temperature sensor

features.heaterHint: Below the minimum the hornet heats by itself and refuses to switch off; above the maximum it switches off and refuses to switch on. One switch-on lasts no longer than set. Sensor lost: 10 min on, 20 min off. Empty field: keep as is.
features.none: Nothing chosen: the hornet leaves these pins alone, measures no temperature, does not heat and does not switch a relay. It stays connected and still reports its battery.
features.notNumber: Heater limits: numbers please, e.g. 5 or 22.5

boards.esp-01-dht11: ESP-01S with a DHT11 sensor (the “ESP-01S DHT11” module)

monitor.hint: Read-only: the latest messages from hornets and the hive. Nothing is sent from here, and no broker login is needed.
monitor.failed: Could not get the messages (admin sign-in needed)

cert.title: Hive certificate (no more browser warning)
cert.hint: The hive serves HTTPS with its own certificate: it has no public name, so the browser warns. Install the hive's root certificate once on each device.

steps.windows: Download the certificate and open the file.|Click "Install Certificate", choose "Local Machine".|Choose "Place all certificates in the following store" → "Trusted Root Certification Authorities".|Restart the browser.
steps.firefox: Open Settings → Privacy & Security → "Certificates" at the bottom → "View Certificates".|"Authorities" tab → "Import" → pick the downloaded file.|Tick "Trust this CA to identify websites" and press OK.|If you added an exception for the hive before, remove it on the "Servers" tab.
steps.android: Download the certificate.|Settings → Security → Encryption & credentials → Install a certificate → CA certificate.|Pick the downloaded file and confirm.
steps.iphone: Open this page in Safari and download the certificate, allow the profile download.|Settings → Profile Downloaded → Install.|Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings → turn the hive certificate on.
steps.mac: Download the certificate and open the file: it goes into Keychain Access.|Find it (Caddy Local Authority), open it, Trust → "Always Trust".|Restart the browser.

cert.once: Once per device: the hive certificate is valid for 10 years. It is needed again only if the hive is reinstalled from scratch.

console.title: Hornet console over USB
console.hint: Connect the board to this computer by USB (Chrome or Edge), press Connect and pick the port. This is what the Arduino IDE serial monitor shows, plus ready-made commands. Speed 115200.
console.unsupported: The USB console works only in Chrome and Edge (Firefox has no Web Serial) and on a secure page: open the hive over https://.
console.connected: Connected. If the board sleeps, restart it (the RESET button or Reset below).
console.openFailed: Could not open the port (is another program using it?)
console.resetHint: Restart the board through the RTS line (not every adapter has it wired)
console.empty: What the board writes to its console appears here. Empty? Check the cable and restart the board.
console.rescue: Rescue: bring the board back to the hive network
console.rescueHint: Writes the Wi-Fi saved in the hive Settings (network name and password) into the board and restarts it. If the board has also forgotten the hive address, write that too.
console.rescueConfirm: Write the network "{ssid}" from the hive Settings into the board?
console.rescueDone: Written. Press Restart the board and watch the output.
console.noHiveWifi: No Wi-Fi network and password are saved in the hive Settings
console.setKeys: Settings: set ssid, set pass, set mqtt, set mqttuser, set mqttpass, set id, set upload, set token, set ntp (the value after a space). For a new hornet: enroll <hive address> <code>.
console.factoryConfirm: Erase ALL settings of the board (network, name, keys)? It will have to be set up again.

cmd.show: What the board has stored: name, network, hive address, boot count and the state of a Wi-Fi switch
cmd.awake: Do not sleep until reboot (for battery boards, to have time to set them up)
cmd.factory: Erase all settings of the board
cmd.enroll: join the hive with a one-time code (Wi-Fi must be set); easier with the Enroll button above

console.join: Enroll the board in the hive
console.joinHint: For a new or replaced board whose id and hive address are empty. Choose the hornet it replaces (the code is issued for you); the hive address comes from Settings. The board gets the Wi-Fi from Settings and the enroll command: it fetches its id, broker address, MQTT login and photo token from the hive itself. The hornet record is kept, so history stays.
console.joinNoUrl: The hive address is not set: type it or set it in Settings
console.joinNeedChoice: Choose a hornet or type a code
console.joinConfirm: Write the Wi-Fi '{ssid}' to the board and join the hive {url}? The board will replace the chosen hornet.
console.joinSent: Commands sent, see the board's answer above: 'enrolled ...'
console.brownout: The board restarted because the supply sagged (brownout). Typical for an ESP32-CAM on a weak USB adapter: the current jumps when Wi-Fi starts. Feed 5 V from a proper supply (1 A or more) to the 5V pin and add a 470 uF capacitor between 5V and GND.
console.notConfigured: The board is not linked to the hive: it has no id and no MQTT login (this happens after the flash was erased, or when only the Wi-Fi and the address were written). Use the Enroll card below: choose the hornet this board replaces and press Issue a code and enroll.

tasmota.intro: For a board that already runs Tasmota or OpenBeken (relay, socket, thermostat). The hive gives it a login of its own, limited to its topics, and the lines for its console. How to flash the board itself: docs/tasmota.md.
tasmota.maxOnHint: The relay switches itself off after this time even if the hive is gone. A timed switch-on from the rules is shorter than this.
tasmota.steps: Connect to the board (a Tasmota board shows as tasmota-XXXX, no password) and give it your home network|Open the board's web page, the Console section|Paste the lines one by one, top to bottom, waiting for the answer after each|The board restarts and shows up in the hive as a hornet
tasmota.passwordOnce: The password is shown once and kept nowhere. Lost it: issue the login again, the previous one stops working.
tasmota.waiting: Waiting for the board to reach the hive.
tasmota.ir: With infrared: a remote, a board with an IR LED and an IR receiver

ir.title: Remote (infrared)
ir.hint: Point the real remote at the board and press a button: its code appears below, give it a name. The hive sends the named buttons itself, for example from a rule. Infrared has no feedback: the hive cannot tell that the device took the command.
ir.learn: Learn a button from the remote
ir.waiting: Waiting for a code: press a button on the remote, pointing it at the board.
ir.unknownProtocol: The protocol was not recognised: this code cannot be sent. Try closer to the board or another button.
ir.alreadySaved: This button is already saved as '{name}'.

ble.title: Bluetooth thermometer
ble.hint: The bridge connects to the kitchen thermometer over Bluetooth and passes its probes on as ordinary temperature. Give the thermometer address. Without one the bridge scans for Bluetooth devices around it and lists them in its log (below on this page).
ble.macEmpty: No address: the bridge scans for devices around it and lists them in the hornet log, below on this page.
ble.dump: Write the thermometer's raw data to the log (to compare the numbers with the Inkbird app)
ble.saved: Saved, the hornet applies it the next time it connects

zigbee.title: Zigbee: dongle and zigbee2mqtt
zigbee.hint: Zigbee sensors and plugs join the dongle on the hive, not Wi-Fi. Allow joining, put the device in pairing mode (most: hold its button for 5 seconds until the LED blinks) and it appears in the list below.
zigbee.bridgeDown: zigbee2mqtt does not answer: check that the container runs and the dongle is plugged in (docs/zigbee.md).
zigbee.none: Nothing yet. Allow joining and put the device in pairing mode.
zigbee.interviewing: The device is being interviewed, wait.
zigbee.unsupported: zigbee2mqtt does not know this model yet: readings may not arrive.
zigbee.added: Added. The first reading arrives when the device reports.
zigbee.off: Zigbee is off. Plug in the dongle and start zigbee2mqtt as in docs/zigbee.md (Zigbee__Enabled).

tasmotaConsole.title: Tasmota console
tasmotaConsole.hint: Administrators only: any Tasmota command goes to the device as typed, for example `RfSend {"Data":"A1B2C3"}` or `PulseTime1 3700`. What the device answers and what it heard by itself (an RF or infrared code) shows up in the hornet log below on this page.
tasmotaConsole.secret: Values of commands with password, key, token or secret in the name are not kept in the command journal.

notes.title: Notes
notes.empty: No notes yet. Create the first one.
notes.pick: Pick a note on the left or create a new one.
notes.dropRoot: Drop here to make it a root
notes.deleteConfirm: Delete “{title}” with its nested notes? It can be restored from the trash for 30 days.
notes.placeholder: Write here. Paste or drop a picture to add it.

cluster.observer: City node: shows a copy of the events. Changes are made on the main node, at home.
cluster.homeDown: Home has not answered for {m} min. Waiting for it.
cluster.standby: Home has not answered for {m} min and hornets write here. The city node has taken over the alarms; rules only notify, commands by hand.

display.title: Screen
display.hint: What the hornet's screen shows: its own readings or those of another device (a thermometer outside, say). The hive refreshes the screen when the readings change.
display.own: Nothing chosen: the screen shows the hornet's own readings (temperature, humidity, voltage).
display.label: Label (optional)
display.saved: Saved, the screen updates within a minute
display.layout: One line: a label and a large value. Two lines: two large values. Three or four: small rows with a label. Readings older than 30 minutes show as "--".

ipcam.intro: Third-party IP cameras recorded by a Dahua NVR. The hive talks to the NVR, not to each camera: it takes motion and snapshots from it. Every channel picked becomes a camera of the swarm that can go into a group and into rules.
ipcam.name: Name, e.g. "House NVR"
ipcam.loginHint: The password is kept encrypted in the hive and never shown back. The NVR locks the login after a few wrong passwords: check with care.
ipcam.pickChannels: Tick the channels that become cameras of the swarm and name them
ipcam.recordWhenDisarmed: Take photos on motion even when disarmed
ipcam.guardHint: Motion when armed: an alarm with three photos in Telegram. "Arriving": a quiet warning. Disarmed: the feed only.
ipcam.deleted: NVR deleted, its cameras left the swarm
ipcam.deleteConfirm: Delete "{name}"? Its cameras leave the swarm, events and photos stay.

errors.auth: The NVR refused the login or password
errors.unreachable: Nothing answers at this address and port
errors.not_dahua: What answers here is not a Dahua NVR
errors.locked: The NVR locked the login after wrong passwords. Wait until it unlocks and check the password

sources.auto: auto: the NVR, then the video stream
sources.rtsp: a frame of the video stream (RTSP)

login.locked: The NVR locked the login, {n} min left. The hive leaves it alone meanwhile so the lock is not extended.
login.paused: The NVR refused the password twice. The hive stopped asking it to avoid a lockout: check the login and save it again.
login.wait: The NVR refused the password ({n} attempts left). Next try in a minute.

stream.connected: Event stream: up since {since}, last signal {last}, reconnects {n}
stream.off: No event stream (no channels, or this hive only watches)

ipcam.adminOnly: The NVR settings are for administrators.
ipcam.nvrGone: This NVR is no longer in the hive settings.
